title: Book 1, Chapter 2 — Causes of the War—The Affair of Epidamnus—The Affair of Potidæa
paragraphs: Epidamnus is a city on the right as one enters the Ionic Gulf. The Taulantians, an Illyrian people, live in the country around it. It is a colony of Corcyra, founded by Phalius, son of Eratocleides, a descendant of Heracles. Following ancient custom, he had been called in from Corinth, the mother country, to lead the settlement. Some Corinthians and others of the Dorian race joined the colonists. As time went on, Epidamnus grew great and populous. But it was torn by factions, said to have arisen from a war with the neighboring barbarians, and it was greatly weakened and lost much of its power. The last event before the war was the expulsion of the nobles by the people. The exiles joined the barbarians and plundered the city by sea and by land. The Epidamnians, hard pressed, sent ambassadors to Corcyra, their mother country, begging her not to let them perish, but to reconcile them with the exiles and free them from the war with the barbarians. The ambassadors sat down as suppliants in the temple of Hera and made these requests to the Corcyraeans. But the Corcyraeans would not accept their supplication, and the ambassadors were sent away with nothing accomplished.

When the Epidamnians saw that they could expect no help from Corcyra, they did not know what to do. So they sent to Delphi and asked the god whether they should hand their city over to the Corinthians and try to obtain some help from their founders. He answered that they should hand it over and put themselves under Corinthian protection. So the Epidamnians went to Corinth and surrendered the colony, obeying the oracle. They pointed out that their founder had come from Corinth, they revealed the god’s answer, and they begged the Corinthians not to let them perish but to help them. The Corinthians agreed. They considered the colony to belong to themselves as much as to the Corcyraeans, and they felt it a kind of duty to protect it. They also hated the Corcyraeans for despising their mother country. Every other colony gave the parent city the usual honors at public assemblies, such as precedence at sacrifices. Corcyra gave Corinth none, and treated her with contempt. Yet Corcyra was as wealthy as any of the richest communities in Hellas, possessed great military strength, and at times could not hide its pride in the naval standing of an island whose seafaring fame went back to its old inhabitants, the Phaeacians. This was one reason why the Corcyraeans lavished so much care on their fleet, which became very efficient. Indeed, they began the war with a force of a hundred and twenty galleys.

All these grievances made Corinth eager to send the promised help to Epidamnus. She advertised for volunteer settlers and sent off a force of Ambraciots, Leucadians and Corinthians. They went by land to Apollonia, a Corinthian colony, avoiding the sea route for fear of interference from the Corcyraeans. When the Corcyraeans learned that settlers and troops had reached Epidamnus and that the colony had been surrendered to Corinth, they were furious. They put to sea at once with twenty-five ships, soon followed by others, and insolently ordered the Epidamnians to take back the banished nobles and to dismiss the Corinthian garrison and settlers. (It must be explained that the Epidamnian exiles had come to Corcyra, pointed to the tombs of their ancestors, and appealed to their kinsmen to restore them.) The Epidamnians paid no attention to any of this. The Corcyraeans then began operations against them with a fleet of forty ships. They took the exiles with them, intending to restore them, and also enlisted the Illyrians. They encamped before the city and proclaimed that any of the natives who wished, and the foreigners, could leave unharmed, and that otherwise they would be treated as enemies. When no one accepted, the Corcyraeans besieged the city, which stands on an isthmus. Meanwhile the Corinthians, hearing that Epidamnus was under siege, assembled an armament and proclaimed a colony to Epidamnus, with perfect political equality guaranteed to all who chose to go. Anyone not ready to sail at once could pay fifty Corinthian drachmae and have a share in the colony without leaving Corinth. Great numbers took up the offer, some ready to start immediately, others paying the sum required. In case the Corcyraeans disputed their passage, several cities were asked to supply an escort. Megara prepared to accompany them with eight ships, Pale in Cephallonia with four; Epidaurus furnished five, Hermione one, Troezen two, Leucas ten, and Ambracia eight. The Thebans and Phliasians were asked for money, the Eleans for empty hulls as well; and Corinth herself supplied thirty ships and three thousand heavy infantry.

When the Corcyraeans heard of these preparations, they went to Corinth with envoys from Lacedaemon and Sicyon, whom they had persuaded to come along. They told the Corinthians to recall the garrison and settlers, since Corinth had nothing to do with Epidamnus. If Corinth did have any claims, they said, they were willing to submit the matter to arbitration by whichever cities in Peloponnese both sides agreed on, and the colony would remain with the city the arbitrators assigned it to. They were also willing to refer the matter to the oracle at Delphi. But if Corinth ignored their protests and appealed to war, they would be forced by this violence to look for friends in quarters where they did not wish to look, and to let even old ties give way to the need for help. Corinth answered that if the Corcyraeans withdrew their fleet and the barbarians from Epidamnus, negotiation might be possible; but while the town was still besieged, going before arbitrators was out of the question. The Corcyraeans replied that if Corinth withdrew her troops from Epidamnus, they would withdraw theirs. Or they were ready to leave both sides as they were, with an armistice concluded until judgment could be given.

The Corinthians rejected all these proposals. Their ships were now manned and their allies had come in. They sent a herald ahead to declare war, and set out with seventy-five ships and two thousand heavy infantry, sailing for Epidamnus to fight the Corcyraeans. Aristeus, son of Pellichas, Callicrates, son of Callias, and Timanor, son of Timanthes, commanded the fleet; Archetimus, son of Eurytimus, and Isarchidas, son of Isarchus, commanded the troops. They reached Actium in the territory of Anactorium, at the mouth of the Gulf of Ambracia, where the temple of Apollo stands. There the Corcyraeans sent a herald ahead in a light boat to warn them not to sail against them. Meanwhile the Corcyraeans began manning their ships, all of which had been fitted out for action, the old vessels having been braced with undergirding to make them seaworthy. The herald came back with no peaceful answer from the Corinthians, and the Corcyraean ships were now manned. They put out to sea against the enemy with a fleet of eighty ships (forty were engaged in the siege of Epidamnus), formed line, and went into action. They won a decisive victory and destroyed fifteen of the Corinthian ships. On the same day the besiegers forced Epidamnus to capitulate, on condition that the foreigners be sold and the Corinthians held as prisoners of war until their fate should be decided.

After the battle the Corcyraeans set up a trophy on Leukimme, a headland of Corcyra, and killed all their captives except the Corinthians, whom they kept as prisoners of war. The Corinthians and their allies, defeated at sea, went home, and left the Corcyraeans masters of all the sea in those parts. The Corcyraeans sailed to Leucas, a Corinthian colony, and ravaged its territory. They also burned Cyllene, the harbor of the Eleans, because the Eleans had furnished ships and money to Corinth. For almost the whole period after the battle they remained masters of the sea, and Corcyraean cruisers harassed the allies of Corinth. At last Corinth, roused by her allies’ sufferings, sent out ships and troops in the late summer. They made an encampment at Actium and near Chimerium, in Thesprotis, to protect Leucas and the other friendly cities. The Corcyraeans for their part formed a similar station on Leukimme. Neither side made any move. They stayed facing each other until the end of the summer, and winter was near before either returned home.

Corinth was exasperated by the war with the Corcyraeans. For the whole of the year after the battle and the year after that, she spent her effort building ships and straining every nerve to form an efficient fleet, drawing rowers from Peloponnese and the rest of Hellas with the lure of large bounties. The Corcyraeans were alarmed at the news of these preparations. They had not a single ally in Hellas, for they had enrolled themselves in neither the Athenian nor the Lacedaemonian confederacy. They decided to go to Athens, make an alliance, and try to obtain support from her. Corinth, hearing of their intentions, also sent an embassy to Athens. She wanted to prevent the Athenian navy from joining the Corcyraean, since that would obstruct her hope of ordering the war as she wished. An assembly was called, and the rival advocates appeared. The Corcyraeans spoke as follows:

“Athenians! When a people has rendered no important service or support to its neighbors in the past, such as it could claim to be repaid for, and then appears before them as we now appear before you to ask for their help, it may fairly be required to meet certain preliminary conditions. It should show, first, that granting its request is expedient, or at least safe; next, that it will keep a lasting sense of the kindness. If it cannot clearly establish any of these points, it must not be annoyed if it meets with a rebuff. Now the Corcyraeans believe that along with their petition for help they can give you a satisfactory answer on these points, and so they have sent us here. As it happens, our policy toward you in making this request turns out to be inconsistent, and as regards our own interests, at the present crisis, inexpedient. We say inconsistent, because a power that has never in all its past history been willing to ally itself with any of its neighbors is now found asking them to ally themselves with it. And we say inexpedient, because in our present war with Corinth that policy has left us entirely isolated. What once seemed the wise precaution of refusing alliances with other powers, so as not to be drawn into risks of their choosing, has now proved to be folly and weakness. It is true that in the recent naval engagement we drove the Corinthians back from our shores single-handed. But they have now gathered a still larger armament from Peloponnese and the rest of Hellas. We see that we cannot possibly cope with them without foreign aid, and that subjection to them would mean immense danger. So we find it necessary to ask help from you and from every other power. We hope to be excused if we give up our old principle of complete political isolation. We did not adopt it with any sinister intention; it was rather the result of an error in judgment.

“Now there are many reasons why, if you comply, you will congratulate yourselves that this request was made to you. First, your help will go to a power which does no harm itself and is the victim of the injustice of others. Secondly, everything we value most is at stake in the present contest, so that your welcome of us in these circumstances will be a proof of goodwill, and the gratitude you earn will stay alive in our hearts forever. Thirdly, you excepted, we are the greatest naval power in Hellas. Moreover, can you imagine a stroke of good fortune more rare in itself, or more disheartening to your enemies? Here is a power whose adhesion you would have valued above much material and moral strength. It presents itself unasked, delivers itself into your hands without danger and without expense, and puts you in the way of winning a high reputation in the eyes of the world, the gratitude of those you assist, and a great increase of strength for yourselves. You may search all history without finding many instances of a people gaining all these advantages at once. Few are the powers that come seeking assistance and are able to give the people whose alliance they ask as much safety and honor as they receive. But it will be said that we shall be useful only in the case of war. To this we answer that if any of you imagines that war is far off, he is grievously mistaken. He is blind to the fact that Lacedaemon regards you with jealousy and wants war, and that Corinth is powerful there. Remember, this is the same Corinth that is your enemy, and that is even now trying to subdue us as a preliminary to attacking you. She does this to keep us from becoming united by a common enmity, so that she will not have us both on her hands, and also to make sure of getting the start of you in one of two ways: either by crippling our power or by making its strength her own. Now it is our policy to be ahead of her, that is, for Corcyra to offer an alliance and for you to accept it. In fact, we ought to make plans against her, instead of waiting to defeat the plans she makes against us.

“If she asserts that it is not right for you to receive a colony of hers into alliance, let her know that every colony that is well treated honors its parent state, but is estranged from it by injustice. For colonists are not sent out to be the slaves of those who stay behind, but to be their equals. And that Corinth was injuring us is clear. Invited to refer the dispute about Epidamnus to arbitration, they chose to pursue their complaints by war rather than by a fair trial. Let their conduct toward us, who are their kindred, be a warning to you not to be misled by their deceit, nor to yield to their direct requests. Concessions to adversaries only end in self-reproach, and the more firmly they are refused, the greater the chance of safety.

“If it is urged that receiving us will be a breach of the treaty between you and Lacedaemon, the answer is that we are a neutral state, and that one of the express provisions of that treaty is that any neutral Hellenic state may join whichever side it pleases. And it is intolerable that Corinth should be allowed to obtain men for her navy not only from her allies but also from the rest of Hellas, no small number being furnished by your own subjects, while we are to be shut out both from the alliance left open to us by treaty and from any help we might get from other quarters, and you are to be accused of political immorality if you grant our request. On the other hand, we shall have much greater cause to complain of you if you refuse it: if we, who are in peril and are no enemies of yours, meet with a rebuff at your hands, while Corinth, the aggressor and your enemy, not only meets with no hindrance from you but is even allowed to draw material for war from your dependencies. This ought not to be. You should either forbid her to enlist men in your dominions, or you should lend us too whatever help you think advisable.

“But your real policy is to give us open countenance and support. The advantages of this course, as we said at the beginning of our speech, are many. We mention one that is perhaps the chief. Could there be a clearer guarantee of our good faith than this: the power that is at enmity with you is also at enmity with us, and that power is fully able to punish defection? And there is a wide difference between declining the alliance of an inland power and of a maritime one. Your first endeavor should be to prevent, if possible, the existence of any naval power except your own; failing this, to secure the friendship of the strongest that does exist. And if any of you believe that what we urge is expedient but fear to act on that belief lest it lead to a breach of the treaty, you must remember two things. Whatever your fears, your strength will be formidable to your antagonists; and whatever the confidence you draw from refusing to receive us, your weakness will have no terrors for a strong enemy. You must also remember that your decision is for Athens no less than for Corcyra. You are not making the best provision for Athens’ interests if, at a time when you are anxiously scanning the horizon to be ready for the war that is all but upon you, you hesitate to attach to your side a place whose adhesion or estrangement is equally pregnant with the most vital consequences. For Corcyra lies conveniently for coastal navigation toward Italy and Sicily, able to bar naval reinforcements from there to Peloponnese and from Peloponnese to there; and in other respects it is a most desirable station. To sum up as shortly as possible, embracing both general and particular considerations, let this show you the folly of sacrificing us. Remember that there are but three considerable naval powers in Hellas, Athens, Corcyra and Corinth. If you allow two of these three to become one, and Corinth to secure us for herself, you will have to hold the sea against the united fleets of Corcyra and Peloponnese. But if you receive us, you will have our ships to reinforce you in the struggle.”
Such were the words of the Corcyraeans. When they had finished, the Corinthians spoke as follows:

“These Corcyraeans, in the speech we have just heard, do not confine themselves to the question of their reception into your alliance. They also talk of our being guilty of injustice and of their being the victims of an unjustifiable war. We must touch on both these points before we go on to the rest of what we have to say, so that you may have a more correct idea of the grounds of our claim and good cause to reject their petition. According to them, their old policy of refusing all offers of alliance was a policy of moderation. In fact it was adopted for bad ends, not for good. Their conduct is such that they have no wish to have allies present to witness it, or to bear the shame of asking for their concurrence. Besides, their geographical situation makes them independent of others. Consequently, when they injure anyone, the decision lies not with judges appointed by mutual agreement but with themselves, because they seldom sail to their neighbors, while foreign vessels are constantly being forced to put in at Corcyra. In short, the object they set themselves with their specious policy of complete isolation is not to avoid sharing in the crimes of others, but to keep a monopoly of crime for themselves: the license to outrage wherever they can compel, to defraud wherever they can elude, and to enjoy their gains without shame. And yet if they were the honest men they pretend to be, the less hold others had upon them, the more clearly they could have shown their honesty by giving and taking what was just.

“But such has not been their conduct either toward others or toward us. Our colony has always been estranged from us and is now hostile. They say: ‘We were not sent out to be ill-treated.’ We reply that we did not found the colony to be insulted by them, but to be their head and to be regarded with proper respect. At any rate our other colonies honor us, and we are much loved by our colonists. Clearly, if the majority are satisfied with us, these few can have no good reason for a dissatisfaction in which they stand alone; and we are not acting improperly in making war against them, nor are we making war without having received signal provocation. Besides, if we were in the wrong, it would be honorable in them to give way to our wishes, and disgraceful for us to trample on their moderation. But in the pride and license of wealth they have sinned against us again and again, and never more deeply than over Epidamnus, our dependency. They took no steps to claim it in its distress when we came to relieve it; they seized it instead, and now hold it by force of arms.

“They allege that they wanted the question first submitted to arbitration. But it is obvious that a challenge from the party who is safe in a commanding position cannot earn the credit due only to the man who, before appealing to arms, puts himself on a level with his adversary in deeds as well as words. In their case, it was not before they laid siege to the place, but after they finally understood that we would not tamely suffer it, that they thought of the specious word arbitration. And not satisfied with their own misconduct there, they now appear here asking you to join with them, not in alliance but in crime, and to receive them in spite of their enmity with us. But they should have made overtures to you when they stood firmest, and not at a time when we have been wronged and they are in peril. Nor should they come at a time when you would be admitting to a share in your protection those who never admitted you to a share in their power, and when you would be incurring from us the same amount of blame as those in whose offenses you had no hand. No, they should have shared their power with you before they asked you to share your fortunes with them.

“So the reality of the grievances we have come to complain of, and the violence and rapacity of our opponents, have both been proved. But you have still to learn that you cannot equitably receive them. It may be true that one provision of the treaty is that any state whose name was not on the list may join whichever side it pleases. But this agreement is not meant for those who join in order to injure other powers. It is meant for those whose need of support does not arise from defection, and whose adhesion will not bring war instead of peace to the power that is mad enough to receive them. That will be the case with you, if you refuse to listen to us. For you cannot become their auxiliary and remain our friend. If you join in their attack, you must share the punishment which the defenders inflict on them. And yet you have the best possible right to be neutral, or, failing this, you should on the contrary join us against them. Corinth is at least in treaty with you; with Corcyra you were never even in truce. But do not lay down the principle that defection is to be patronized. Did we record our vote against you when the Samians defected, and the rest of the Peloponnesian powers were equally divided on whether to assist them? No, we told them to their face that every power has a right to punish its own allies. Why, if you make it your policy to receive and assist all offenders, you will find that just as many of your dependencies will come over to us, and the principle you establish will press less heavily on us than on yourselves.

“This, then, is what Hellenic law entitles us to demand as a right. But we also have advice to offer and claims on your gratitude. Since there is no danger of our injuring you, as we are not enemies, and since our friendship does not amount to very frequent intercourse, we say that these claims ought to be settled at the present juncture. When you needed warships for the war against the Aeginetans, before the Persian invasion, Corinth supplied you with twenty vessels. That good turn, and the line we took on the Samian question, when we were the reason the Peloponnesians refused to assist them, enabled you to conquer Aegina and to punish Samos. And we acted thus at crises when, if ever, men are apt to forget everything for the sake of victory in their efforts against their enemies. They regard the man who assists them then as a friend, even if he has been a foe until now, and the man who opposes them then as a foe, even if he has been a friend until now. Indeed they allow their real interests to suffer from their absorbing preoccupation with the struggle.

“Weigh well these considerations. Let your youth learn what they are from their elders, and let them resolve to do to us as we have done to you. And let them not acknowledge the justice of what we say but dispute its wisdom in the event of war. Not only is the straightest path generally the wisest; but the coming of the war, which the Corcyraeans have used as a bugbear to persuade you to do wrong, is still uncertain, and it is not worth being carried away by it into winning the immediate and declared enmity of Corinth. It would be wiser, rather, to try to counteract the unfavorable impression which your conduct toward Megara has created. For kindness shown at the right moment has a greater power to remove old grievances than the facts of the case may warrant. And do not be seduced by the prospect of a great naval alliance. Abstaining from all injustice to other first-rate powers is a greater tower of strength than anything that can be gained by sacrificing permanent tranquillity for an apparent temporary advantage. It is now our turn to benefit by the principle that we laid down at Lacedaemon, that every power has a right to punish her own allies. We now claim to receive the same from you, and we protest against your rewarding us for benefiting you by our vote by injuring us with yours. On the contrary, return us like for like, remembering that this is the very crisis in which he who lends aid is most a friend, and he who opposes is most a foe. And as for these Corcyraeans, neither receive them into alliance in spite of us, nor be their abettors in crime. Do this, and you will act as we have a right to expect of you, and at the same time best consult your own interests.”
Such were the words of the Corinthians.

The Athenians heard both sides and held two assemblies. In the first, they clearly leaned toward the arguments of Corinth. In the second, opinion changed, and they decided to make an alliance with Corcyra, with certain reservations. It was to be defensive, not offensive. It did not break the treaty with Peloponnese, since Athens could not be required to join Corcyra in an attack on Corinth. But each party had a right to the other’s help if either its own territory or that of an ally was invaded. For people had begun to feel that the Peloponnesian war was only a matter of time, and no one was willing to see a naval power as great as Corcyra sacrificed to Corinth. If the two could be left to wear each other down in mutual conflict, that would be no bad preparation for the struggle that Athens might one day have to fight with Corinth and the other naval powers. At the same time, the island seemed well placed on the coasting route to Italy and Sicily. With these views, Athens took Corcyra into alliance. Not long after the Corinthians departed, she sent ten ships to help the Corcyraeans. Their commanders were Lacedaemonius, son of Cimon, Diotimus, son of Strombichus, and Proteas, son of Epicles. Their orders were to avoid a clash with the Corinthian fleet, except in certain circumstances: if it sailed to Corcyra and threatened to land on her coast or on any of her possessions, they were to do their utmost to stop it. These orders came from a concern not to break the treaty.

Meanwhile the Corinthians finished their preparations and sailed for Corcyra with a hundred and fifty ships. Elis supplied ten of these, Megara twelve, Leucas ten, Ambracia twenty-seven, Anactorium one, and Corinth herself ninety. Each contingent had its own admiral; the Corinthian one was commanded by Xenoclides, son of Euthycles, with four colleagues. They sailed from Leucas and made land on the part of the continent opposite Corcyra. They anchored in the harbor of Chimerium, in the territory of Thesprotis. At some distance from the sea above it lies the city of Ephyre, in the Elean district, and by this city the Acherusian lake pours its waters into the sea. The lake takes its name from the river Acheron, which flows through Thesprotis and falls into it. The river Thyamis also flows there, forming the boundary between Thesprotis and Kestrine, and the point of Chimerium rises between these two rivers. In this part of the continent the Corinthians anchored and made a camp. When the Corcyraeans saw them coming, they manned a hundred and ten ships, under the command of Meikiades, Aisimides and Eurybatus, and took up position at one of the Sybota isles, with the ten Athenian ships present. On Point Leukimme they stationed their land forces, together with a thousand heavy infantry who had come to help them from Zacynthus. The Corinthians on the mainland did not lack allies either. The barbarians came in large numbers to help them, since the inhabitants of this part of the continent were old allies of theirs.

When their preparations were complete, the Corinthians took three days’ provisions and put out from Chimerium by night, ready for action. They sailed at dawn and sighted the Corcyraean fleet out at sea, coming toward them. As soon as the two sides saw each other, they formed in order of battle. On the Corcyraean right wing lay the Athenian ships; the rest of the line was held by the Corcyraeans’ own vessels, in three squadrons, each commanded by one of the three admirals. This was the Corcyraean formation. The Corinthian formation was as follows. On the right wing lay the Megarian and Ambraciot ships, and in the center the rest of the allies in order. The left was made up of the best sailers in the Corinthian navy, to meet the Athenians and the right wing of the Corcyraeans. As soon as the signals were raised on either side, they joined battle. Both sides had large numbers of heavy infantry on their decks, and large numbers of archers and darters, since the old, imperfect armament was still in use. The sea-fight was stubborn, though not remarkable for skill; in fact it was more like a battle on land. Whenever ships charged each other, the number of vessels and the crush made it far from easy to break loose. Besides, their hopes of victory lay mainly in the heavy infantry on the decks, who stood and fought in order while the ships stayed still. The maneuver of breaking the line was not tried. In short, strength and spirit counted for more in the fight than skill. Tumult reigned everywhere, and the battle was one scene of confusion. Meanwhile the Athenian ships kept coming up to the Corcyraeans whenever they were pressed, and so alarmed the enemy, though their commanders could not join the battle because they feared their orders. The right wing of the Corinthians suffered most. The Corcyraeans routed it with twenty ships and chased it in disorder to the continent. They sailed up to the Corinthian camp, burned the tents, which they found empty, and plundered the baggage. So in this quarter the Corinthians and their allies were defeated and the Corcyraeans were victorious. But where the Corinthians themselves were, on the left, they won a decided success, since the scanty Corcyraean forces were weakened further by the absence of the twenty ships away in the pursuit. When the Athenians saw the Corcyraeans hard pressed, they began at last to help them more openly. At first, it is true, they held back from charging any ship. But when the rout was becoming plain and the Corinthians were pressing on, the time finally came when everyone set to, all distinctions were dropped, and it came to this: Corinthians and Athenians raised their hands against each other.

After the rout, the Corinthians did not bother to lash fast and tow away the hulls of the vessels they had disabled. Instead they turned on the men, whom they butchered as they sailed through, caring less to take prisoners. They even killed some of their own friends by mistake, not knowing that their right wing had been defeated. For the number of ships on both sides, and the distance over which they covered the sea, made it hard, once the fleets had joined, to tell conquerors from conquered. This battle proved far greater than any before it, at least any between Hellenes, in the number of vessels engaged. After the Corinthians had chased the Corcyraeans to land, they turned to the wrecks and their dead. They succeeded in getting hold of most of these and conveying them to Sybota, the meeting place of the land forces supplied by their barbarian allies. Sybota, it must be said, is a desert harbor of Thesprotis. When this task was over, they mustered again and sailed against the Corcyraeans. The Corcyraeans advanced to meet them with all the ships they had left that were fit for service, accompanied by the Athenian vessels, for they feared that the Corinthians might attempt a landing in their territory. It was by now getting late, and the paean had been sung for the attack, when the Corinthians suddenly began to back water. They had seen twenty Athenian ships sailing up. The Athenians had sent these out afterward to reinforce the ten, fearing, as it turned out justly, that the Corcyraeans would be defeated and that their handful of ships could not protect them. The Corinthians saw these ships first. They suspected that they were from Athens and that those they saw were not all, but that more were behind. So they began to retire. The Corcyraeans had not sighted the ships, since they were advancing from a point where they could not see so well. They were wondering why the Corinthians were backing water when some caught sight of the Athenians and cried out that there were ships in view ahead. At this they also retired, for it was now getting dark, and the Corinthian retreat had suspended the fighting. So the two sides parted, and the battle ceased with night. The Corcyraeans were in their camp at Leukimme when these twenty ships from Athens, under the command of Glaucon, son of Leagrus, and Andocides, son of Leogoras, made their way through the corpses and wrecks and sailed up to the camp, not long after they had been sighted. It was now night, and the Corcyraeans feared that they might be hostile vessels. But they soon recognized them, and the ships came to anchor.

The next day the thirty Athenian vessels put out to sea, together with all the Corcyraean ships that were seaworthy, and sailed to the harbor at Sybota, where the Corinthians lay, to see whether they would fight. The Corinthians put out from the land and formed a line in the open sea, but went no further, since they had no intention of taking the offensive. For they saw that fresh reinforcements had arrived from Athens and that they themselves faced numerous difficulties: they had to guard the prisoners they had on board, and in a desert place they had no means of refitting their ships. They were thinking more about how their voyage home was to be managed. They feared that the Athenians might consider the treaty dissolved by the collision that had occurred, and forbid them to leave.

So they resolved to put some men on board a boat and send them to the Athenians without a herald’s wand, as an experiment. Having done so, the men spoke as follows: “You do wrong, Athenians, to begin war and break the treaty. We are punishing our enemies, and we find you putting yourselves in our path, in arms against us. Now if you intend to prevent us from sailing to Corcyra, or anywhere else we wish, and if you are set on breaking the treaty, first take us who are here and treat us as enemies.” This is what they said, and all the Corcyraean armament within hearing immediately called out to take them and kill them. But the Athenians answered as follows: “We are not beginning war, Peloponnesians, and we are not breaking the treaty. These Corcyraeans are our allies, and we have come to help them. So if you want to sail anywhere else, we place no obstacle in your way; but if you are going to sail against Corcyra, or any of her possessions, we shall do our best to stop you.”

On receiving this answer from the Athenians, the Corinthians began preparing for their voyage home, and set up a trophy at Sybota, on the continent. The Corcyraeans, for their part, picked up the wrecks and dead that the current, and a wind that rose in the night, had scattered in all directions and carried out to them, and as victors they set up their own trophy at Sybota, on the island. Each side had its own reasons for claiming the victory. The Corinthians had been victorious in the sea-fight until night. This had enabled them to carry off most of the wrecks and dead, and they held no fewer than a thousand prisoners of war, and had sunk close upon seventy vessels. The Corcyraeans had destroyed about thirty ships, and after the Athenians arrived they had picked up the wrecks and dead on their own side. They had also seen the Corinthians retire before them, backing water at the sight of the Athenian vessels, and, once the Athenians had come, refuse to sail out against them from Sybota. So both sides claimed the victory.

On the voyage home the Corinthians took Anactorium, which stands at the mouth of the Ambracian gulf. They took the place by treachery, since it was common ground to the Corcyraeans and the Corinthians. After settling Corinthians there, they went home. Of the Corcyraean prisoners, eight hundred were slaves, and these they sold. Two hundred and fifty they kept in captivity, treating them with great attention in the hope that on their return they might bring their country over to Corinth; most of them happened to be men of very high position in Corcyra. In this way Corcyra kept her political existence in the war with Corinth, and the Athenian vessels left the island. This was the first cause of the war that Corinth had against the Athenians, namely that they had fought against her alongside the Corcyraeans in time of treaty.

Almost immediately after this, fresh differences arose between the Athenians and the Peloponnesians, and added their share to the war. Corinth was forming schemes for retaliation, and Athens suspected her hostility. The Potidæans, who inhabit the isthmus of Pallene, were a Corinthian colony but tributary allies of Athens. They were ordered to raze the wall on the side toward Pallene, to give hostages, to dismiss the Corinthian magistrates, and in future not to receive the men whom Corinth sent each year to succeed them. The Athenians feared that Perdiccas and the Corinthians might persuade the Potidæans to revolt, and that they might draw the rest of the allies in the direction of Thrace to revolt with them. The Athenians took these precautions against the Potidæans immediately after the battle at Corcyra. Corinth was now openly hostile, and besides, Perdiccas, son of Alexander, king of the Macedonians, had gone from being an old friend and ally to being an enemy. The Athenians had made him an enemy by allying themselves with his brother Philip and with Derdas, who were in league against him. In his alarm he had sent to Lacedaemon to try to involve the Athenians in a war with the Peloponnesians, and he was trying to win over Corinth in order to bring about the revolt of Potidæa. He also made overtures to the Chalcidians in the direction of Thrace, and to the Bottiaeans, to persuade them to join in the revolt. For he thought that if these places on the border could be made his allies, it would be easier to carry on the war with their cooperation. The Athenians were alive to all this and wished to forestall the revolt of the cities, and so they acted as follows. They were just then sending off thirty ships and a thousand heavy infantry to his country, under the command of Archestratus, son of Lycomedes, with four colleagues. They instructed the commanders to take hostages from the Potidæans, to raze the wall, and to be on their guard against the revolt of the neighboring cities.

Meanwhile the Potidæans sent envoys to Athens, in the hope of persuading the Athenians to take no new steps against them. They also went to Lacedaemon with the Corinthians, to secure support in case of need. After long negotiation they got nothing satisfactory from the Athenians. For all they could say, they could not prevent the ships destined for Macedonia from sailing against them as well. But the Lacedaemonian government promised to invade Attica if the Athenians attacked Potidæa. Favored by this moment, the Potidæans at last entered into league with the Chalcidians and Bottiaeans, and revolted. And Perdiccas induced the Chalcidians to abandon and demolish their towns on the seaboard and to settle inland at Olynthus, making that one city a stronghold. To those who followed his advice he gave part of his own territory in Mygdonia, round Lake Bolbe, as a place to live for as long as the war against the Athenians should last. So they demolished their towns, moved inland and prepared for war. The thirty ships of the Athenians arrived before the Thracian places and found Potidæa and the rest in revolt. Their commanders considered it quite impossible, with their present force, to make war on Perdiccas and on the allied towns as well. They therefore turned to Macedonia, their original destination, established themselves there, and carried on the war in cooperation with Philip and the brothers of Derdas, who had invaded the country from the interior.

Meanwhile the Corinthians, with Potidæa in revolt and the Athenian ships on the coast of Macedonia, were alarmed for the safety of the place and thought its danger their own. They sent volunteers from Corinth, and mercenaries from the rest of Peloponnese, sixteen hundred heavy infantry in all, and four hundred light troops. Aristeus, son of Adimantus, took command of the expedition. He had always been a steady friend to the Potidæans, and it was mainly out of love for him that most of the men from Corinth volunteered. They arrived in Thrace forty days after the revolt of Potidæa.

The Athenians also received news of the revolt of the cities at once. When they learned that Aristeus and his reinforcements were on their way, they sent two thousand heavy infantry of their own citizens and forty ships against the places in revolt, under the command of Callias, son of Calliades, and four colleagues. They arrived in Macedonia first, and found the force of a thousand men sent out earlier, who had just become masters of Therme and were besieging Pydna. So they too joined in the siege of Pydna, and kept it up for a while. Afterward they came to terms and made a forced alliance with Perdiccas, being hurried by the calls from Potidæa and by the arrival of Aristeus there. They withdrew from Macedonia, going to Beroea and from there to Strepsa. After a futile attempt on Strepsa, they continued their march by land to Potidæa, with three thousand heavy infantry of their own citizens, a number of their allies, and six hundred Macedonian horsemen, the followers of Philip and Pausanias. Seventy ships sailed along the coast with them. They advanced by short marches, and on the third day they reached Gigonus, where they encamped.

Meanwhile the Potidæans and the Peloponnesians with Aristeus were encamped on the isthmus, on the side facing Olynthus, waiting for the Athenians, and they had set up their market outside the city. The allies had chosen Aristeus general of all the infantry, and the command of the cavalry was given to Perdiccas. He had at once left the alliance of the Athenians and gone back to that of the Potidæans, and had appointed Iolaus as his general. The plan of Aristeus was to keep his own force on the isthmus and await the Athenian attack. The Chalcidians and the allies were to stay outside the isthmus, and the two hundred cavalry of Perdiccas at Olynthus, to act on the Athenian rear when the Athenians advanced against him, so that the enemy would be placed between two fires. Meanwhile Callias the Athenian general and his colleagues sent the Macedonian horse and a few of the allies to Olynthus, to prevent any movement from that quarter. The Athenians themselves broke up their camp and marched against Potidæa. When they reached the isthmus and saw the enemy preparing for battle, they formed against him, and soon afterward the two sides engaged. The wing of Aristeus, with the Corinthians and other picked troops around him, routed the wing opposed to it and followed it a considerable distance in pursuit. But the rest of the army of the Potidæans and Peloponnesians was defeated by the Athenians and took refuge inside the fortifications. When Aristeus returned from the pursuit, he saw that the rest of the army was defeated. He was at a loss which of two risks to choose, whether to go to Olynthus or to Potidæa. In the end he decided to draw his men into as small a space as possible and force his way into Potidæa at a run. Not without difficulty, through a storm of missiles, he passed along the breakwater through the sea, and brought off most of his men safe, though a few were lost. Meanwhile the auxiliaries of the Potidæans from Olynthus, which is about seven miles off and in sight of Potidæa, had advanced a little way to help when the battle began and the signals were raised, and the Macedonian horse had formed against them to prevent it. But victory soon declared for the Athenians and the signals were taken down, and the auxiliaries retired back within the wall, while the Macedonians returned to the Athenians. So there were no cavalry present on either side. After the battle the Athenians set up a trophy and gave back their dead to the Potidæans under truce. The Potidæans and their allies had close upon three hundred killed; the Athenians had a hundred and fifty of their own citizens killed, and Callias their general.

The Athenians at once raised works against the wall on the side of the isthmus and manned them. The wall on the side of Pallene had no works raised against it. They did not think themselves strong enough both to keep a garrison on the isthmus and to cross over to Pallene and raise works there, for they were afraid that the Potidæans and their allies might take advantage of their division to attack them. Meanwhile the Athenians at home learned that there were no works at Pallene, and some time afterward they sent off sixteen hundred heavy infantry of their own citizens under the command of Phormio, son of Asopius. He arrived at Pallene and fixed his headquarters at Aphytis. From there he led his army against Potidæa by short marches, ravaging the country as he advanced. No one ventured to meet him in the field, and he raised works against the wall on the side of Pallene. So at length Potidæa was strongly invested on both sides, and from the sea by the ships cooperating in the blockade. Aristeus saw that the investment was complete. He had no hope of saving the place, except through some movement from Peloponnese or some other improbable chance. He advised all but five hundred to watch for a wind and sail out of the place, so that the provisions might last longer, and he was willing to be one of those who stayed. He could not persuade them. He wanted to take the next best course and to have things outside in the best state possible, so he eluded the Athenian guardships and sailed out. He remained among the Chalcidians and continued to carry on the war. In particular, he laid an ambush near the city of the Sermylians and cut off many of them. He also communicated with Peloponnese, and tried to contrive some way by which help might be brought. Meanwhile, after the investment of Potidæa was complete, Phormio employed his sixteen hundred men next in ravaging Chalcidice and Bottica, and he also took some of the towns.
